steps.title: Welcome to Monsters Ink!
steps.content:
Learn ink! smart contract development by building and evolving your own digital creature.

How It Works

  • Learn — Complete lessons to master ink! fundamentals
  • Build — Write real smart contracts that compile and deploy
  • Evolve — Watch your creature transform as your skills grow
  • Own — Mint your evolved creature as an NFT on Polkadot
Your Creature, Your Journey

Your creature reflects your progress as an ink! developer. It evolves with each lesson you complete—permanent on-chain proof of your skills.

Before writing code, let's understand what you're building.

steps.title: What is a Blockchain?
steps.content:
A decentralised computer - a network of computers running a program that ensures all computers run the same logic and store the same data.

What Makes a Blockchain Special?

Instead of one server owned by one company, a blockchain is run by many independent nodes around the world.

Each node:
  • Stores a copy of the data
  • Verifies transactions
  • Agrees on what is true
No single point of failure. No single owner.

How Do Computers Agree?

Blockchains use consensus - rules that decide what data is valid.

If most nodes agree:
  • The data is added
  • The state updates
  • The history becomes permanent
Trying to cheat means convincing thousands of nodes at once. Good luck with that.

Why Does This Matter?

Because blockchains are:
  • Trustless - you don't need to trust anyone
  • Transparent - anyone can verify the rules and data
  • Immutable - history can't be changed
  • Permissionless - anyone can participate

A blockchain doesn't just store data - it enforces rules.
And those rules are written as smart contracts.

Next: Let's understand smart contracts using a simple vending machine

steps.title: What Are Smart Contracts?
steps.content:
The Vending Machine Analogy

Imagine a vending machine:

1. You insert money ($1.50)
2. You press the button (B3)
3. The machine automatically dispenses your snack

No cashier needed! The rules are built into the machine.

A smart contract works the same way:

  • Code defines the rules (like the vending machine's logic)
  • Executes automatically when conditions are met
  • No intermediaries - no middleman required

Why Smart Contracts?

Smart contracts enable public infrastructure where the rules are transparent and accessible to all.

What You Can Build:

AI Agents - AI that owns a wallet, pays for services, enters agreements autonomously
Programmable Games - Rules enforced by code that developers can't change mid-match
Portable Reputation - Your skills and contributions follow you across platforms
Automatic Payments - Funds move when conditions are met (delivery confirmed, milestone hit)
Shared Ownership - Co-own AI models, datasets, compute—contributors paid automatically

Next: Let's learn about ink! - the language we'll use to write Smart Contracts!

steps.title: What is ink!?
steps.content:
ink! is the Rust Smart Contract language for Polkadot.

Why ink!?

Built on Rust - One of the safest programming languages

Memory safe - No buffer overflows or null pointer bugs
Type safe - Catches errors at compile time
Fast - Performance close to C/C++
Modern - Great tooling, developer experience and Community!
New to Rust? Don't worry! We'll teach you what you need.

For deeper learning, check out:
- The Rust Book
- Rustlings - Interactive exercises
- ink! Official Docs

Next: Let's break down the ink! contract structure!

chapters.title: ink! Contract Anatomy
chapters.description: Learn the building blocks of every ink! contract: storage, constructors, and messages

steps.title: The Contract Module
steps.content:
Every ink! contract starts with this foundation. Let's break it down line by line.

Line 1: Compiler Configuration

#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std, no_main)]

This tells Rust: "When compiling for blockchain, don't use standard library."

Think of it as "blockchain mode" - we're compiling to PolkaVM bytecode, not for your computer.

Line 3: The ink! Macro

#[ink::contract]

This is a macro - a special Rust feature that transforms your code.

It takes your contract and adds all the blockchain capabilities automatically.

Line 4-6: The Module

mod creature {
  // Your contract code goes here!
}

This is a Rust module - a namespace for your contract's code.

Everything related to your contract lives inside here.

Key Takeaway: These 6 lines are the skeleton of every ink! contract. You'll write them every time.
steps.hint: This is the foundation of every ink! contract. No changes needed - just understand each line!

steps.title: Storage: Your Contract's Memory
steps.content:
Storage is your contract's permanent memory on the blockchain.

What is Storage?

Think of storage like a hard drive for your contract:

Persists forever on the blockchain
Costs gas to write (modifying costs money)
Free to read
Defined using a struct with the #[ink(storage)] macro

Example: Storage for a Monster

#[ink(storage)]
pub struct Monster {
    is_awake: bool,        // Is the monster awake?
    energy: u32,           // Energy level (0-100)
    owner: AccountId,     // Who owns this monster?
}

Breaking It Down:

  • #[ink(storage)] - Tells ink! "this struct is the contract's storage"
  • pub struct Monster - Creates a public structure named Monster
  • is_awake: bool - A field that stores true/false
  • energy: u32 - A field that stores a number (0 to 4,294,967,295)
  • owner: AccountId - A field that stores a blockchain address
Rule of Thumb: Storage = The data your contract remembers between transactions.

Next: Let's learn how to create (construct) a contract.

steps.title: Constructors: Birthing Contracts
steps.content:
Constructors are functions that run once when your contract is deployed.

What is a Constructor?

Think of constructors as the birth certificate of your contract:

Runs exactly once when the contract is deployed
Sets up initial storage values
Can accept parameters (like initial configuration)
Multiple allowed - different ways to deploy

Example: Constructor for a Monster

#[ink(constructor)]
pub fn new() -> Self {
    Self {
        is_awake: false,
        energy: 100,
        owner: Self::env().caller(),
    }
}

Breaking It Down:

  • #[ink(constructor)] - Marks this function as a constructor
  • pub fn new() - Public function named "new" (convention, but you can name it anything)
  • -> Self - Returns an instance of the contract (the struct)
  • Self { ... } - Creates and returns the contract with initial values
  • Self::env().caller() - Gets the address of whoever is deploying the contract

Multiple Constructors:

#[ink(constructor)]
pub fn new_awake() -> Self {  // Alternative constructor
    Self {
        is_awake: true,        // Born awake!
        energy: 50,
        owner: Self::env().caller(),
    }
}
Key Takeaway: Constructors initialize your contract's storage when it's first deployed.

Next: Let's learn about messages - how to interact with your contract.

steps.title: Messages: Contract Functions
steps.content:
Messages are functions you can call after your contract is deployed.

Two Types of Messages:

1. Read Functions (Getters) - Using &self

Only read data from storage
FREE - No gas cost
Instant - No blockchain transaction
Example: "Is my monster awake?"

#[ink(message)]
pub fn is_awake(&self) -> bool {
    self.is_awake  // Just return the value
}
2. Write Functions (Setters) - Using &mut self

Can modify storage data
Costs gas - You're changing the blockchain
Takes time - Requires blockchain confirmation
Example: "Wake up my monster!"

#[ink(message)]
pub fn wake_up(&mut self) {
    self.is_awake = !self.is_awake;  // Toggle
}

The Critical Difference:

&self &mut self
Can modify storage? No Yes
Costs gas? Free Costs gas
Speed Instant Requires confirmation
Golden Rule:

Use &self when you just want to look
Use &mut self when you want to change

Complete Example:

impl Monster {
    // READ: Get energy level
    #[ink(message)]
    pub fn get_energy(&self) -> u32 {
        self.energy
    }

    // WRITE: Feed the monster
    #[ink(message)]
    pub fn feed(&mut self) {
        self.energy += 10;  // Increase energy
    }
}

You now understand the 3 pillars of ink! contracts:

  • Storage - What data your contract remembers
  • Constructors - How your contract is born
  • Messages - How users interact with your contract
Learn More:

- ink! Contract Template
- Storing Values in ink!
- Reading Values
- Mutating Values

chapters.title: Building Your Creature Contract
chapters.description: Write your first complete ink! smart contract step-by-step

steps.title: 🥚 Let's Build Your Creature!
steps.content:
Time to Code! 🧬

You're about to write your first complete ink! smart contract - step by step.

By the end of this chapter, you'll have a working Creature contract and unlock your evolving creature NFT!

🎨 Your Evolving Creature

Complete this chapter to mint your creature NFT.
✨ The same NFT evolves as you complete more lessons
🎓 One creature, one journey - permanent on-chain proof of your growth

Your Task:

No changes needed yet - just recognize the foundation from Chapter 1!
steps.hint: This is your foundation! Every ink! contract needs these lines to work on the blockchain. No changes needed - just understand each line!

steps.title: 🧠 Give Your Creature Memory
steps.content:
Give Your Creature Memory! 🧠

Your creature needs memory to remember if it's awake or sleeping.

Your Task:

Replace the comment with a storage structure that tracks consciousness.

💡 Add these 4 lines:

#[ink(storage)]
pub struct Creature {
    is_awake: bool,
}

This creates permanent memory on the blockchain - your creature will remember its state forever!
steps.hint: Replace the comment with the storage structure. Start with #[ink(storage)], then create the struct with one boolean field!

steps.title: 🏗️ Create Implementation Block
steps.content:
Create the Implementation Block! 🏗️

Now we need to add functions to your creature. First, create the implementation block.

Your Task:

After the struct, add an empty implementation block.

💡 Add these lines after the struct:
impl Creature { }

All your creature's abilities will go inside this block!
steps.hint: Add 'impl Creature { }' after the struct to create a place for your creature's functions!

steps.title: 🐣 Birth Your Creature
steps.content:
Birth Your Creature! 🐣

Every creature needs a way to be born. Let's add a constructor!

Your Task:

Inside the impl block, add a constructor function.

💡 Add inside the impl block:

#[ink(constructor)]
pub fn new() -> Self {
    Self { is_awake: false }
}

Your creature will be born sleeping peacefully... for now! 💤
steps.hint: Add the constructor inside the impl block. Don't forget the #[ink(constructor)] attribute!

steps.title: 📖 Add Default Birth Method
steps.content:
Add a Default Birth Method! 📖

Let's add a second constructor that uses default values. This is a common pattern in ink! contracts.

Your Task:

Add a default constructor after the new() function.

💡 Add after the new() function:

#[ink(constructor)]
pub fn default() -> Self {
    Self::new()
}

This lets users deploy without specifying anything - convenient! ✨
steps.hint: Constructors can delegate to other constructors! This default() constructor just calls new() for convenience.

steps.title: 👁️ Let Your Creature Speak
steps.content:
Let Your Creature Speak! 👁️

Your creature needs to tell others if it's awake or sleeping.

Your Task:

Add a function to check if the creature is awake.

💡 Add after the constructors:

#[ink(message)]
pub fn is_awake(&self) -> bool {
    self.is_awake
}

Remember: &self means read-only, so it's FREE! 💰
steps.hint: This function is a read (getter) function. In ink!, &self means you're only reading data, not changing anything. Add #[ink(message)] above your function to make it callable from outside.

steps.title: 🔄 The Final Power: Wake Up!
steps.content:
The Final Power: Wake Up! 🔄

Give your creature the ultimate ability - to control its own consciousness!

Your Task:

Add a function to toggle the creature's consciousness.

💡 Add after the is_awake function:

#[ink(message)]
pub fn wake_up(&mut self) {
    self.is_awake = !self.is_awake;
}

The ! operator flips the boolean: true → false, false → true

Remember: &mut self because we're modifying storage! ✏️

🌟 Your creature will awaken when you complete this! Watch its eyes open! 👁️
steps.hint: This function is a write (setter) function. In ink!, using &mut self means you want to change the contract's state. The ! operator flips the boolean: true becomes false and vice versa.

chapters.title: Testing & Deployment
chapters.description: Compile, test, and deploy your Flipper contract to the blockchain

steps.title: 🔨 Understanding Compilation
steps.content:
Compiling Your Contract 🔨

Time to transform your Rust code into blockchain-ready PolkaVM bytecode!

What Happens During Compilation?

📦 Three Artifacts Are Generated:

1. flipper.contract
    → The complete bundle (deploy this!)
    → Contains PolkaVM bytecode + metadata

2. flipper.polkavm
    → Compiled PolkaVM bytecode
    → The actual executable on the blockchain

3. flipper.json
    → Contract metadata (ABI)
    → Describes your contract's interface

Using pop-cli to Build:

pop build

This single command:

  • ✅ Compiles your Rust code to PolkaVM
  • ✅ Optimizes the bytecode for minimal size
  • ✅ Generates the metadata JSON
  • ✅ Bundles everything into a .contract file
💡 Pro Tip: Always build before deploying! The compiler catches many errors before they hit the blockchain.

steps.title: 🚀 Deploying Your Contract
steps.content:
Deploy to the Blockchain! 🚀

Let's bring your Flipper to life on a real blockchain!

Step 1: Start a Local Node

pop up ink-node

This starts a local ink! development node on your computer - like a personal blockchain! 🖥️

Step 2: Deploy the Contract

pop up --constructor new --args "true"

This command:

  • 📤 Uploads your .contract file to the chain
  • 🏗️ Instantiates it using the new(true) constructor
  • 💰 Uses test tokens to pay for deployment
  • 📝 Returns your contract address
🎯 Alternative: Use the default constructor:

pop up --constructor default

This deploys with value = false!
🎉 Your contract is now live! You'll receive a contract address like:
0x8eaf04151687736326c9fea17e25fc5287613693

steps.title: 🎮 Interacting with Your Contract
steps.content:
Call Your Contract! 🎮

Now let's interact with your deployed Flipper contract!

Reading the Value (Free! 💰)

pop call contract --contract <ADDRESS> --message get

This calls the get() function. Since it uses &self, it's a dry-run - no gas needed!

Output:
Result: true

Flipping the Value (Costs Gas ⛽)

pop call contract --contract <ADDRESS> --message flip --execute

The --execute flag means "submit this as a transaction." It:

  • ✅ Modifies blockchain state
  • ✅ Costs gas (test tokens on local chain)
  • ✅ Waits for block confirmation
  • ✅ Returns a transaction hash

Verify the Flip:

pop call contract --contract <ADDRESS> --message get
Output:
Result: false  // It flipped! 🎉

Testing Before Executing:

💡 Pro Tip: Always test with --dry-run first!

pop call contract --contract <ADDRESS> --message flip --dry-run

This simulates the call without spending gas.

Congratulations! 🎊 You've successfully:

  • ✅ Written a complete ink! smart contract
  • ✅ Compiled it to PolkaVM bytecode
  • ✅ Deployed it to a blockchain
  • ✅ Interacted with it using read and write functions
